 Columbus mother of eight turns to food pantries ahead of Thanksgiving after losing SNAP benefits
 BY 
 Aliah Keller
 Columbus 
 PUBLISHED 9:48 AM ET Nov. 14, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 9:48 AM EST Nov. 14, 2026 
 SHARE 
 COLUMBUS, Ohio — With Thanksgiving less than two weeks away, one Columbus mother is trying to figure out how she’ll put a holiday meal on the table for her eight children.
 Laquanda Lipsey says her Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits stopped last week. Now, she’s relying on local food pantries to help feed her family.
 “We have less food. You have to come and come to the food pantry and see what they have there for you and your children,” Lipsey said.
 Lipsey, who is raising her eight children on her own, recently picked up groceries at NNEMAP Food Pantry in Columbus.
 She says she’s still trying to understand why her benefits stopped. She believes it could be related to her children getting older or an issue with renewing her benefits.
 A car accident has also made it difficult for her to work, leaving her with even less money to cover everyday expenses.
 “$600 a month. That’s what I have like to spend just on, like, household items and on food. It’s really not too much,” she said.
 Food pantries see changing needs
 Ohio expanded SNAP work requirements this year, affecting who qualifies for food assistance.
 According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, about 140,000 fewer Ohioans received SNAP benefits in July compared to the same month in 2025.
 At NNEMAP Food Pantry, executive director Roy Clark says the number of people coming in for food hasn’t changed, but the types of requests they’re making have.
 “There’s been a lot more people just requesting volunteering hours because they know that that’s something that’s required until they find work,” Clark said.
 Volunteer hours can count toward SNAP work requirements for some recipients.
 But Clark says food pantries can’t always offer the same selection of groceries that families could buy using SNAP benefits.
 “It’s not like a full assortment of food that you would see at a grocery store,” he said.
 For Lipsey, that means visiting other food pantries in the coming days, hoping to find enough food to make Thanksgiving special for her children.
 “I’m gonna still keep hope alive, for sure,” she said. “You know, I have eight kids, so I have to make them happy. You know, it can’t be sad on Thanksgiving.”
